subject: Critical Thinking
title: David Hume: The Great Skeptic of Cause and Effect
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: David Hume: The Great Skeptic of Cause and Effect.

hook.text: The sun has risen every day of recorded history. Will it rise tomorrow?

buildup.text: David Hume's 'problem of induction': past patterns don't logically guarantee future ones.

discovery.text: Hume showed that causation itself is unobservable. You see billiard ball A hit B, then B moves.

twist.text: This doesn't mean science is wrong – it means science rests on assumptions that can't themselves be scientifically.

climax.text: Hume's skepticism was constructive: it forces us to be humble about certainty & precise about what evidence can &.

punchline.text: Correlation isn't causation. Hume proved it 300 years ago.

quiz.question: What is Hume's 'problem of induction'?
options: Past patterns don't logically guarantee future ones; we assume but can't prove continuity

details.summary: David Hume argued that we never actually observe causation — only the regular succession of events. His skepticism about cause and effect shook the foundations of science and philosophy, forcing a rethinking of what knowledge is possible.
details.whyItMatters: Hume's insight that causation is inferred, not observed, remains one of the deepest challenges in epistemology and is foundational to modern philosophy of science.
takeaways: We observe correlation, not causation directly
The problem of induction challenges all empirical knowledge
Hume's skepticism inspired Kant's entire philosophical project

faq.question: What did Hume mean by saying we never observe causation?
faq.answer: We see one billiard ball hit another and the second one move. But we only see sequence and contact, not a 'causal power.' Our belief in causation is a habit of mind created by repeated experience, not a direct observation of a necessary connection.

faq.question: How did Hume's skepticism influence the development of science?
faq.answer: It motivated Karl Popper's falsificationism, inspired probabilistic reasoning in science, and forced scientists to admit that all empirical knowledge is provisional. Hume's challenge is the reason scientists say 'evidence suggests' rather than 'evidence proves.'
